top.title: Bainbridge, Central Kitsap volleyball teams collect trophies
top.description: For the second consecutive season, Bainbridge's volleyball team left the Class 2A state tournament at the Yakima Valley SunDome with a trophy. Placing 7th at state in 2025, the Spartans earned 6th place on Saturday, Nov. 14 after finishing 2-2 during the two-day tournament. Bainbridge wrapped up its season with 21-2 record. Winning the Olympic League title and West Central District championship, Bainbridge drew the No. 5 seed at state and opened Friday with a 3-1 win over No. 12 Mark Morris. The Spartans then lost 3-0 in the quarterfinals against No. 4 Ridgefield, which ended up winning the 2A title over No. 2 Ellensburg. On Saturday, Bainbridge won 3-1 against No. 9 Orting in an elimination match before the Spartans fell 3-0 against No. 3 Pullman in the 5th/6th-place game. North Kitsap (13-8) qualified for state as well. The Vikings went 0-2, dropping 3-1 matches against Pullman and No. 11 Selah. Central Kitsap tops Timberline for district title Central Kitsap will head to next week's 3A state tournament in Yakima with plenty of momentum. The Cougars captured the West Central District championship Saturday at Mount Tahoma High School by knocking off Timberline 3-1. It was the Blazers' first defeat of the season. In the semifinals, Central Kitsap beat defending 3A champion North Thurston 3-1. Central Kitsap (18-3) will learn its state seed on Sunday when the 3A brackets are released. The 3A tournament runs Nov. 20-21. The Cougars placed 6th last season. This article originally appeared on Kitsap Sun: Bainbridge, Central Kitsap volleyball teams collect trophies

On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
top.description: null On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) Why it mattered When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later. "In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus." The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO. The Green Bank Telescope collapse left a mass of twisted debris behind. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions. "One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website. Want more space history? Five Falcons will be among the most tested in this matchup. Michael Penix Jr. The formidable Chiefs defense will be another big test for Michael Penix, thanks to defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo. Spags’ strategy will likely lean on blitzing Penix to exploit his struggles under pressure and using disguised coverages to confuse the young quarterback. For Penix’s evaluation, it’s important to see how he handles one of the NFL’s most challenging defensive schemes and stays poised amid the controlled chaos. Bijan Robinson Bijan Robinson, along with the Falcons’ run game, will be tasked with taking pressure off Penix, but will be tested against one of the NFL’s best run defenses. Whatever category you want to measure, whether it’s yards, yards per carry, EPA, or yards before and after contact, the Chiefs rank among the top 10 teams across the board . That looks impressive at face value, but his success rate in those games was 36 percent, which ranks among the bottom 5 in the NFL, according to NextGenStats . As the NFL’s leading rusher, Robinson has racked up most of his production against lesser defenses, averaging 115 yards per game, 5.6 yards per carry, with a second-ranked 52 percent success rate in his five other outings. Essentially, the numbers show that the quality of competition dictates the Falcons’ success when establishing the run. Given the Chiefs’ stout defense, it’s another huge trial to see whether this trend continues. top.title: Triumph or flop? The Rugby League World Cup that split opinion
top.description: The winning captains: Australia's Isabelle Kelly, her men's counterpart Isaah Yeo and England wheelchair skipper Lewis King [Getty Images] Has the 2026 Rugby League World Cup been a success or not? It depends on who you listen to - and perhaps where in the world you are. The men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments provided plenty of stories - from Kalyn Ponga's return from a broken arm in 23 days, to Jodie Cunningham's mangled ear, to the England wheelchair team's golden ladder, to the men's group format that caused widespread bafflement. But was the World Cup a triumph? The northern and southern hemisphere perspectives provide contrasting answers. For the fourth tournament running, Australia won the men's and women's titles, with New Zealand unable to deliver a twist in either final. Tonga and Samoa brought vibrancy and passion - performing to a level that underlined why they are being elevated to Tier One status. The large Polynesian population in the USA - which will co-host the 2030 men's and women's World Cups - is likely to be key in spreading the rugby league word further around the world. England's Wheelchair World Cup win, in a thunderous final against their old foes France, offset some of the disappointment felt when Brian McDermott's men and Stuart Barrow's women went home early. And unlike when the game was emerging from post-pandemic constraints in 2022, the tournament has also worked financially by posting a profit. "This whole tournament's been incredible," said Australia men's captain Isaah Yeo. "Not just the fans here for New Zealand and Australia, but just everyone. I thought it was all outstanding. "I think it's to date the most competitive and the best World Cup there's been. I think that's only going to continue to grow." That sentiment has been endorsed repeatedly by Australian television broadcaster Channel Seven, which paid a reported A$12m (£6.1m) for exclusive domestic free-to-air coverage of the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments. Not everyone has been able to feel that positivity, though. The decision to cut the men's tournament from 16 teams to 10 reduced the overall number of matches - and deprived teams such as Jamaica and Greece of a chance to build on the feelgood factor they provided as debutants in 2022. That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons. For those who did get to the party this time, it has not always been an even contest. The disparity between the haves and have-nots has been significant. While the Jillaroos and Kangaroos players will each receive equal payments of $40,000 (£20,500) for competing, Wales will reportedly spread a total of $15,000 (£7,689) across their women's and wheelchair teams. top.title: Zverev claims first win as world number one at ATP Finals
top.description: Alexander Zverev has won 66 ATP Tour matches this season - the most of any men's player [Getty Images] Alexander Zverev claimed his first victory as world number one as he swept aside Rafael Jodar in the opening match of the ATP Finals. Germany's Zverev produced a serving masterclass to beat the fast-rising Spaniard 6-4 6-4. The French and US Open champion dropped only 10 points on serve, landing an astonishing 84% of first serves and hitting 10 aces. The only time Zverev looked troubled was when he went two break points down as he served for the opening set - before saving them with back-to-back aces. "I still think I have a lot of things to improve. It was not a perfect match but to start the tournament, I am very happy," the 29-year-old said. "Winning always helps, but it's been a good match." Zverev lost his first match as world number one at the Paris Masters in November and said afterwards he was "annoyed" at the reaction to his rise to the top of the rankings. He has taken full advantage of a year in which Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner have struggled with injuries, winning two majors and reaching the Wimbledon final. Zverev underlined his status as the world's best player by walking out on court in Turin in a custom black leather jacket with a number one printed on the back. His performance was just as befitting of his position as he put constant pressure on the Jodar serve and dominated with his own first strike. The 20-year-old Jodar is one of the brightest talents in the men's game, having started the year outside the world's top 150. Now ranked 11th, he fought hard to stay in touch with Zverev, but could find no way through his serve. Zverev broke him early in the first set with a fine backhand down the line and went up a quick break in the second. He had three further chances for a double-break lead but Jodar saved them, before Zverev served out victory. In the doubles, Britain's Henry Patten and Finnish partner Harri Heliovaara began their campaign with a 6-3 5-7 10-4 win over Brazilian pair Rafael Matos and Orlando Luz. Wimbledon champions Patten and Heliovaara are the defending champions in Turin. Pochettino targets Craven Cottage skipper to plug leaky backline According to The Telegraph , Fulham defender Calvin Bassey has emerged as a surprise candidate to bolster Manchester United's porous defence when the transfer window reopens in January. Appointed last week to replace Michael Carrick , Pochettino has wasted little time assessing the personnel at Old Trafford and views a new centre-half as a top priority. Securing the 26-year-old Nigeria international will prove far from straightforward, however. The former Rangers and Ajax defender enters the final year of his current contract, though the west London club hold an option to extend his stay by a further 12 months. top.title: What Paul McGinley noticed about Tyrrell Hatton’s behavior during the final round in Dubai
top.description: Photo by Richard Heathcote/Getty Images Tyrrell Hatton won the sixth Rolex Series event of his career on Sunday in Dubai after he clinched the DP World Tour Championship at the Earth Course. Hatton played some truly wonderful golf this week in Dubai, especially during the final round as he posted a score of 66 to win the tournament by five shots. Unfortunately for the 35-year-old, his victory procession over the back nine seemed like nothing more than a subplot as Rory McIlroy and Eugenio Chacarra battled it out for the Race to Dubai title. However, Tyrrell Hatton won’t care about that whatsoever. Hatton admitted to being ‘weirdly nervous’ before the final round in Dubai on Sunday, but he obviously harnessed those feelings to good use. Now he can call himself a six-time Rolex Series winner. What Paul McGinley noticed about Tyrrell Hatton’s behavior in Dubai After Hatton’s victory at the Earth Course on Sunday, Sky Sports commentators Paul McGinley and Nick Dougherty highlighted how they noticed a big change in the Englishman’s behavior during the final round. “ I would say personally, watching him across the last two days, he looked a little bit more restrained, “ Dougherty said. “ He looked a little bit more in control of his emotions. It looked like it was a peak Hatton, across those last two days. He really was head shoulders above across the tournament this week. “ Then McGinley chimed in with his opinion on the matter. “ Yeah, I think your point that better behavior from him results in better golf is the correct one. I see that, “ McGinley replied. “ When he got control of the tournament and got ahead, the moaning and groaning seemed to stop, and he seemed to go into overdrive, and he was a little softer on himself. “ You know, he ran off with it, he lapped the field with a five-shot lead. Everybody else got distracted with the Race to Dubai, and he just kept going forward. “ Perhaps Tyrrell Hatton has reached an age now where he has become slightly more easygoing. It was obvious to see that he wasn’t as harsh on himself during the final round in Dubai as he usually is. And if his new-found positive attitude resulted in the golf we saw him produce this week, he may well be a real force in the professional game over the next decade or so.

top.title: When Michael Jordan’s agent revealed Nike’s $3 million fail-safe if Bulls legend flopped
top.description: Photo by Bongarts/Getty Images Nike took all measures in Michael Jordan failed to become a global basketball superstar. When the Chicago Bulls selected Michael Jordan using the third overall pick in the 1984 NBA Draft, no one knew he would become a global sensation. Evidently, when Jordan signed a groundbreaking deal with Nike that included a signature shoe and royalties, it shocked the NBA community to its core. At the time, Nike wasn’t a gigantic corporation, and if trusting MJ had failed, it could have spelt trouble for the company. As a result, Nike tried to play it safe, as revealed by MJ’s agent, David Falk. David Falk once revealed Nike’s escape clause for Michael Jordan During a 2023 appearance on ‘The 20 & 20 Podcast,’ Falk revealed details about his conversation with Nike’s then-marketing head, Rob Strasser. Falk revealed how Nike wanted to insert stat-based clauses in Jordan’s contract with the sneaker company. “That makes no sense. You’re not an NBA team; what do you care what his statistics are? All you should care about is how many shoes he’s selling. “He said, ‘I’ll give you a number. If in the end of the third year, as we head into the fourth year, if we haven’t sold $3 million worth of shoes, we want to be able to stop making the shoe.’ I said no problem,” Falk recalled. He added, “We’ll honor the contract for the full five years, we’ll pay him every dollar he’s owed, but if he doesn’t make Rookie of the Year in his rookie year, or in the first three years, he doesn’t average 20 points a game ever, doesn’t ever make the All-Star team, we want to be able to stop making the shoe.” That $3 million target was Nike’s fail-safe in case Jordan never became a superstar. However, Falk then revealed how the Chicago Bulls guard smashed Nike’s expectations. “They thought selling 3 million will be like hitting a grand slam home run, and Michael sold 126 million in the first year. He sold roughly 40 percent probably of all Nike shoes,” Falk stated. Today, the Jordan Brand is a massive money-making machine for Nike and reportedly generates over $7 billion in annual revenue. top.title: How Bayern Munich and Lennart Karl overcame public disagreements
top.description: MUNICH, GERMANY - FEBRUARY 21: (EDITORS NOTE: Image has been digitally enhanced.) (Photo by Sebastian Widmann/Bundesliga/Bundesliga Collection via Getty Images) Bayern Munich’s honorary president Uli Hoeneß’s recent public criticism of Lennart Karl met with mixed reactions. On one hand, many people acknowledged the Bayern winger’s drop in form and his need to improve. On the other hand, there were those who disliked making such thoughts public. Lennart Karl’s camp certainly did not like these comments, with agent Michael Ballack publicly putting both Hoeneß and later board member for sport Max Eberl on blast . It seemed like something of a schism could form between Karl and Bayern’s management. Fortunately, calmer heads seem to have prevailed. Bild reports (as captured by @iMiaSanMia ) that both sides have already moved past the issue: Following Uli Hoeneß’ public comments criticizing Lennart Karl, an internal meeting took place between sporting director Christoph Freund and Karl’s representatives. During the meeting, Bayern made it clear that they are satisfied with Karl’s development. With his remarks, Hoeneß’ demands from Karl were clear: less unnecessary showboating off the pitch and a bigger focus on football. Karl’s agent, Michael Ballack, subsequently spoke out, publicly defending his client. But, following the internal meeting, both sides want to put their public disagreements behind them and look ahead. It certainly seems like a whole lot of fuss that did not need to become so public, but it has been settled. All is well that ends well, but Bayern does need to make sure Karl is not thrust into the spotlight for such negative reasons again in the coming months. At Agbogbloshie, a district on the Korle Lagoon delta, thousands of tonnes of refuse have accumulated over decades, overwhelming the fragile wetlands overlooking a slum of around 80,000 residents, many of them migrants and traders. For scrap dealer James Hassan, a 31-year-old Liberian immigrant, it is both his home and livelihood. Without gloves or a mask, he sifts daily through piles of unwanted electronics and metal for scraps to sell. The skin on his palms is thickened and scarred from cuts and rashes but he has become accustomed to the pain and discomfort. “I have headaches and coughs after long days under the sun, but I have never sought medical care. I feel they are normal,” he told AFP. Environmental health experts say that workers are exposed to toxic metals and chemicals through skin cuts, inhaling waste smoke and dust. nigeria.title: Meet African countries home to some of the world’s oldest universities
nigeria.description: Africa is home to some of the world’s oldest centres of higher learning, with educational institutions that began centuries before many of the universities commonly associated with Europe’s academic history. From Islamic centres of scholarship in North Africa to historic institutions in West Africa, the continent has a long tradition of organised education, research and intellectual development. Some of these institutions started as mosques and religious schools before evolving into universities, while others emerged as colleges during the 19th century. Here are six African countries home to some of the world’s oldest universities and higher-learning institutions. 1. Tunisia – Ez-Zitouna University (737 AD) Tunisia is home to Ez-Zitouna University, one of the oldest centres of higher learning in the world, with an educational history dating back to the eighth century. Located in Tunis, the institution traces its origins to the Great Mosque of Ez-Zitouna, founded in 734 AD. According to the university’s official historical account, the teaching of Islamic sciences began there around 737 AD. Over the centuries, the institution became an important centre for Islamic scholarship, teaching subjects including Islamic jurisprudence, philosophy, mathematics, medicine and astronomy. It also attracted prominent scholars, including the renowned North African historian Ibn Khaldun, who studied at the institution. Ez-Zitouna remains an important institution for Islamic studies and is widely regarded as one of the oldest continuously operating educational traditions in the Arab and Islamic world. 2. Founded in 859 AD, Al-Qarawiyyin was established as a mosque and centre of learning by Fatima al-Fihri, a Muslim woman who reportedly used her inheritance to finance its construction. The institution gradually developed into a major centre of Islamic scholarship, attracting students and scholars from different parts of Africa and beyond. Its academic activities historically covered Islamic theology, law, Arabic grammar, mathematics and astronomy, among other subjects. Al-Qarawiyyin’s historical significance extends beyond its age. nigeria.title: List of African countries that have their own unique calendars
nigeria.description: Several African countries have calendars that are distinct from the Gregorian calendar, either because they maintain traditional systems of dating or because their religious and cultural communities follow their own calendars. The most notable example is Ethiopia, which has a separate calendar system used for official civil purposes. Other countries have indigenous or religious calendars that remain culturally significant, although they are not necessarily used for government administration. African countries with unique calendar systems 1. Ethiopia – Ethiopian (Ge’ez) Calendar Ethiopia operates a calendar that is approximately seven to eight years behind the Gregorian calendar. It has 13 months : 12 months of 30 days and a final month called Pagume, which has five or six days. Its New Year usually falls on September 11. 2. Egypt – Coptic Calendar The Coptic calendar descends from the ancient Egyptian calendar and is still used by the Coptic Orthodox Church. It has 13 months, with 12 months of 30 days and a short 13th month. Its New Year is known as Nayrouz. 3. Eritrea – Ge’ez Calendar Eritrean Orthodox Christians follow the Ge’ez calendar, which is closely related to Ethiopia’s calendar. Its New Year is called Kidus Yohannes and is celebrated around September 11. Eritrea uses the Gregorian calendar for official administration. 4. Morocco – Amazigh (Berber) Calendar The Amazigh calendar is used traditionally by Berber communities. It follows an agricultural year and marks its New Year, Yennayer, around January 12–14. Morocco recognises Yennayer as a public holiday. 5. Algeria – Amazigh Calendar Algeria also observes the Amazigh agricultural calendar. Yennayer marks the beginning of the traditional year and is celebrated as an important cultural occasion. 6. Nigeria – Igbo Traditional Calendar The Igbo calendar, known as Ọgụ́àfọ̀ Ị̀gbò, has 13 months in its traditional structure. Its week consists of four market days: Eke, Orie, Afọ and Nkwọ. It is used in traditional religious, cultural and market activities, although different Igbo communities may calculate it differently. 7. Ghana – Akan Calendar The Akan people use a traditional 42-day cycle known as Adaduanan, combining a six-day week and a seven-day week. It helps determine traditional festivals, ceremonies and important cultural events. Similar practices are found among Akan communities in Côte d’Ivoire. nigeria.title: More than 900 US flights cancelled Sunday after Friday’s ground stop
nigeria.description: …FAA expects flight schedules to recover by late Sunday By Juliet Umeh More than 900 flights scheduled for Sunday in the United States had been cancelled by late Saturday as airlines continued to recover from a nationwide ground stop imposed by the Federal Aviation Administration, FAA. FlightAware, a flight-tracking service, recorded 910 cancellations for Sunday, with the figure rising. More than 6,400 flights were cancelled on Saturday, following about 9,200 on Friday. The FAA order halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours on Friday. Although it was lifted that evening, passengers continued to face cancellations and delays as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said, “I do think the worst is behind us,” but added that “a significant amount of recovery work” remained. He apologised to travellers, saying: “I’m sorry that we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons.” US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the disruption began during work to replace old copper telecommunications lines with fibre-optic cables at an FAA facility. A router involved in the upgrade overloaded parts of the network, affecting air traffic communications and radar systems. “We had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” Duffy said, adding that the surge caused “issues with our communication with airplanes” and disrupted radar feeds. Officials are investigating whether the problem resulted from an installation error or faulty equipment. “We haven’t determined what the fault was,” Duffy said. Bedford said airlines expected to restore their schedules by late Sunday. “Based on everything that we’re hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they’ll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday,” he said. The FAA said it ordered the ground stop as a safety measure after communications problems affected 17 of its 22 en-route air traffic control centres. Bedford said, “No facilities went dark. Nothing was fully lost.” He also said there was “zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related.” The post More than 900 US flights cancelled Sunday after Friday’s ground stop appeared first on Vanguard News .

nigeria.title: Meta fined €805m for accessing users’ photos, videos without consent
nigeria.description: Italian regulators fined Facebook parent company Meta 805 million euros ($880 million) for accessing users’ photos without their “specific” consent, the country’s data protection authority said on Saturday. Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users “without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them”, the authority said in a statement. Meta said it would appeal the decision. A company spokesperson said “we strongly disagree” with the assessment by the regulators “and the disproportionate level of the fine”. In late October, authorities in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for having misled the state’s residents for more than a decade over use of their data — a record fine for the company, which slammed it as a “tax” on freedom of expression. Saturday’s latest fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant. In 2021, Amazon received a more than 1.1-billion-euro fine for breaching competition law. That sum was subsequently reduced to 752 million euros on appeal. – Facebook gallery feature – The Italian penalty imposed on Facebook relates to its gallery suggestions feature, available since 2023, which suggests photos and videos from a user’s phone gallery as ideas for posts as they are browsing. According to Italy’s regulator, Facebook requested access to the gallery via a single authorisation valid for the entire app, preceded by a generic notice requesting enabling of other features, which did not allow users to understand that they were also authorising suggestions from their gallery. The regulator said Meta would now have to seek consent by means of a separate and specific request for the feature concerned and clearly signpost what it is used for, namely that it involves access to a user’s photo gallery, as well as how to disable it. In determining the size of the fine, the authority said it took into account “the high number of people affected” — around 20 million Android users in Italy — and the duration of the infringement, “which is still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system”. The authority also cited “Meta’s lack of cooperation during the investigation”. It imposed a fine amounting to roughly 0.4 per cent of the group’s annual turnover, which hit $201 billion in 2025, for a net profit of $60.5 billion. entertainment.title: Professor Patricia Mamko Lar Makes History as First Female Vice-Chancellor of UNIJOS
entertainment.description: Professor Patricia Mamko Lar, appointed as the 11th substantive Vice-Chancellor and first female Vice-Chancellor of the University of Jos. The University of Jos (UNIJOS) has officially appointed Professor Patricia Mamko Lar as its 11th substantive Vice-Chancellor, making her the first woman to occupy the position since the institution was established in 1971. Announced on Thursday, 12 November 2026 by the university’s Pro-Chancellor and Chairman of Council, Senator Grace Folashade Bent , during a special meeting of the 15th Governing Council, the historic appointment sees Professor Lar succeed Professor Tanko Ishaya as she takes the helm of the Plateau State institution. Born in Langtang, Plateau State, Professor Lar is a distinguished Professor of Medical Microbiology whose career has been deeply woven into the fabric of UNIJOS for nearly four decades. After earning her Bachelor of Science degree in Microbiology from Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria in 1986, she joined the University of Jos in 1987 as a Graduate Assistant in the Department of Medical Microbiology. She later went on to earn her Master’s degree in Medical Microbiology in 1989 and her PhD in Medical Parasitology in 1998 from the University of Lagos, followed by postdoctoral training at the Institute of Human Virology, University of Maryland in the United States under the NIH-Fogarty Fellowship Programme. Rising steadily through the academic ranks, she became an Associate Professor in 2012 before attaining full professorship in October 2015. Over the years, she has built an impressive body of work with more than 40 scholarly publications focusing on infectious diseases, including HIV/AIDS, malaria, antimicrobial resistance, and phytomedicine. Beyond the lecture hall and laboratory, Professor Lar has also served in key administrative roles at UNIJOS—including Head of the Department of Microbiology and Director of Linkages and Collaborations—and previously served a six-month tenure as Acting Vice-Chancellor of Yakubu Gowon University (formerly the University of Abuja) following her appointment by President Bola Tinubu in February 2025. Alongside her academic and leadership credentials, Professor Lar is a recognised advocate for women’s empowerment, having received the He4She Certificate of Award for Women Empowerment Activism in 2019. As she begins her five-year single term as UNIJOS’s first female substantive Vice-Chancellor after 55 years, she brings nearly four decades of institutional experience to the university’s top seat. entertainment.description: The future of every society is sitting in our classrooms, growing up in our homes and navigating a world that is changing faster than ever before. But an important question confronts parents, educators and society: Are we truly preparing our children for the future, or are we simply raising them for the world we once knew? This is the conversation the Train The Trainers Summit (TTTS) Lagos Edition seeks to ignite when it convenes on Saturday, 28 November 2026, at the D’Podium International Event Centre, Aromire, Ikeja, off Adeniyi Jones, Lagos. Under the compelling theme, Empowering Our Generation Next Leaders: Raising Children to Thrive and Lead, the summit will bring together diverse experts, thought leaders, educators, parents and child development advocates for an important gathering focused on the future of children and the responsibilities of those raising them. Powered by Duke’s Infant & Child Foundation , the summit is built around a powerful conviction: children do not become confident, responsible and capable leaders by accident. They must be intentionally nurtured, properly guided, adequately protected and equipped with the skills and values required to navigate life. Today’s children are growing up in a world of artificial intelligence, digital exposure, changing social influences, emotional pressures, evolving relationships and unprecedented opportunities. While the world is changing, the responsibility of parents, teachers and other adults must also evolve. Speaking at the summit, the convener, Augusta Anyanwu- Egbom said “The question is no longer simply whether children are going to school. It is whether they are developing the emotional intelligence, resilience, critical thinking, digital awareness, identity, confidence and values needed to thrive beyond the classroom.” The Lagos Edition promises an engaging and insightful experience featuring diverse experts and speakers across parenting, education, technology, child psychology, social-emotional development, identity, safety, inclusion and other critical areas of child development. Participants can expect thought-provoking keynote conversations, fireside chats, practical demonstrations, interactive learning sessions and expert-led engagements addressing issues that families, schools and communities can no longer afford to ignore. From understanding the realities of modern parenting to navigating technology and digital safety; from protecting children against harmful influences to strengthening their emotional and social development, the summit will confront difficult questions and explore practical ways to create better outcomes for Generation Next. It will also challenge the traditional assumption that raising children is the responsibility of parents and teachers alone. entertainment.title: Team Nigeria Records Its Best-Ever Youth Olympic Gold Medal Haul at Dakar 2026
entertainment.description: Nigerian sprint champions Praise Tejiri Ugoh, Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo, and Gift Bright celebrate their historic gold medal victories at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. Photo Credit: MakingOfChamps Team Nigeria delivered an unforgettable chapter at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal, wrapping up a historic multi-sport gathering that marked the first time an Olympic-branded event was ever hosted on African soil. Spanning across vibrant venues in Dakar, Diamniadio, and Saly, the Games brought together thousands of young athletes across 25 sports in a true celebration of youth culture, elite competition and unity. The grandeur of the international sporting festival kicked off with a breathtaking opening ceremony at the packed Abdoulaye Wade Stadium in Diamniadio. The night dazzled spectators with rich West African cultural displays, vibrant musical showcases, and a live performance by Nigerian music artist Ibquake , who brought incredible flair to the historic arena alongside global digital stars like Khaby Lame . Amidst the festive atmosphere, the Nigerian delegation walked with immense pride, led by sprint prodigy Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo carrying the national flag. Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo rejoices on the track wrapped in the green and white national flag after securing the women’s 100m gold. Photo Credit: MakingOfChamps/Instagram When the action shifted to the tracks at the Complexe Iba Mar Diop, Team Nigeria turned the athletics arena into a showcase of pure speed, finishing their campaign with a total of three medals—all of them gold. Fifteen-year-old Gift Bright set the blazing pace by conquering the men’s 100m final in a personal-best and Games-record time of 10.28 seconds, earning the distinction of becoming the first Nigerian men’s 100m champion at the Youth Olympics. Gift Bright powers down the track en route to winning the men’s 100m gold in a personal-best 10.28 seconds. Photo Credit: MakingOfChamps/Instagram Matching that stellar brilliance, flagbearer Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo blazed across the finish line in the women’s 100m final in 11.16 seconds, completing a phenomenal sprint double that crowned Nigeria as the first nation in Youth Olympic history to sweep both 100m titles at a single edition. The golden sweep was officially sealed by sixteen-year-old Praise Tejiri Ugoh , who stormed through the women’s 400m final in a personal-best time of 52.76 seconds to claim gold and become the first Nigerian to conquer the 400m distance at the Games. Praise Tejiri Ugoh claims gold for Nigeria on the podium following the women’s 400m final at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. Photo Credit: MakingOfChamps/Instagram These remarkable achievements by Gift Bright, Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo, and Praise Tejiri Ugoh not only surpassed Nigeria’s previous best tally of two gold medals from the inaugural Singapore 2010 Games, but also firmly established the country’s rising track stars as global names to watch. entertainment.title: Ramla Ali Wins IBF and WBO Titles to Become Somalia’s First Boxing World Champion
entertainment.description: Unified world champion Ramla Ali poses in the ring with her WBO and IBF super-bantamweight belts and her coaching team in Arlington, Texas. Photo Credit: Yahya Ali/Instagram British-Somali boxer and fashion model Ramla Ali is officially a unified world champion! On 8 November 2026 at the College Park Center in Arlington, Texas, the 37-year-old athlete captured the vacant IBF and WBO super-bantamweight world titles after securing a split-decision victory over American contender Mikiah Kreps . During the ten-round bout, Ali dropped Kreps with a sharp right hand in the third round—the sole knockdown of the night—before two judges scored the contest 97–92 and 96–93 in her favour, against one scorecard of 98–91 for Kreps. With this triumph, Ali became Somalia’s first-ever professional boxing world champion and a unified titleholder in one unforgettable night. Born in Mogadishu, Somalia, she fled the civil war as a child with her family and grew up in East London, initially taking up boxing in secret as a teenager before turning it into a life-changing calling. Ramla Ali makes her ring walk behind the Somali and British flags ahead of her super-bantamweight world title fight in Arlington, Texas. Photo Credit: Yahya Ali/Instagram Her remarkable journey from refugee to Olympic athlete and champion is also the subject of the biographical feature film In the Shadows. Directed by Anthony Wonke , the film premiered at the 70th BFI London Film Festival on 9 October 2026 before opening in UK and Irish cinemas on 30 October—just over a week before she lifted her world title belts in Texas. BAFTA-winning Top Boy actress Jasmine Jobson stars as Ali alongside Peaky Blinders actor Finn Cole as her husband and former coach, Richard Moore , with both Ali and Moore serving as executive producers on the project. This championship milestone builds on a string of barrier-breaking firsts across sports, cinema, and fashion. Long before her title win in Arlington, Ali made history as the first Muslim woman to win an English amateur boxing title, the first boxer to win an international gold medal while representing Somalia, and the first boxer to represent Somalia on the Olympic stage when she competed in the women’s featherweight division at the Tokyo 2020 Summer Olympics. Ramla Ali celebrates in the ring as the referee raises her hand following her split-decision victory over Mikiah Kreps on 8 November 2026. Photo Credit: Yahya Ali/Instagram Away from the ring, she has carved out an equally notable space in global luxury fashion. Ali has graced the covers of British Vogue, Elle UK, Harper’s Bazaar Arabia, and Grazia UK, served as a brand ambassador for Cartier and Dior, and made history as the first boxer to wear custom ring attire created by major fashion houses—including bespoke fight kits designed by Dior, Off-White, Versace, Alexander McQueen, and Burberry featuring the panther emblem from Somalia’s coat of arms. entertainment.title: Mark Your Calendars! Lagos International Theatre Festival Returns to MUSON Centre This November
entertainment.description: The Lagos International Theatre Festival ( LITF ) returns for its 2026 edition on November 14–15 at the MUSON Centre, Lagos, bringing together an exciting programme of theatre from Nigeria and around the world. The festival, which attracts more than 25,000 attendees across its programme days, has become one of the most anticipated events on Lagos’s cultural calendar. This year’s festival is themed “The Masks We Wear”, anchored by the statement “The Stage Is Everywhere.” The theme explores the different roles and identities people assume in everyday life, while inviting audiences to consider how theatre extends beyond the traditional stage. LITF 2026 brings an international dimension to Lagos, featuring artists and productions from Kenya, Canada and Brazil alongside a diverse Nigerian programme. An international highlight is LeRa Entertainments’ Under The Mango Tree from Canada, produced by Lennette Randall , with productions from Norway, Kenya and Brazil adding further cultural and theatrical perspectives. The Nigerian programme features productions from Lagos, Abuja, Enugu and Abeokuta, including Monkey Laundry , directed by Olarotimi Fakunle ; tHERapy , directed by Tosin Adeyemi ; What You Have Become , directed by Lanre Adediwura; and Behind Closed Doors , directed by Bolanle Austen-Peters. The festival will also spotlight emerging theatre makers through productions from Atlantic Hall, Evergreen College and Children’s International School, alongside professional and independent productions. The festival experience begins ahead of the main weekend with a series of events across Lagos. On November 9, Theatre Meets Food, hosted by Hilda Baci, will bring together artists, partners, cultural leaders and members of Lagos’s creative community for an evening of food, theatre and conversation. This will be followed by Embassy Nights on November 10 and 11, celebrating international cultural exchange among diplomatic representatives, artists and creative industry leaders. The programme culminates in an Opening Night Gala on November 13, ahead of the main festival weekend at MUSON Centre on November 14 and 15. LITF 2026 is supported by the Lagos State Government, LekOil, Pillar Oil, Afrexim and Amstel , alongside its growing network of international and cultural partners. Founder of LITF, Bolanle Austen-Peters , said: “The Masks We Wear is a theme that speaks to all of us. We all play different roles in our lives, and theatre allows us to examine those roles, question them, and perhaps see ourselves differently. This year, we are also reminding audiences that theatre is not confined to a theatre building. The stage is everywhere.” Festival Director, Vanessa Jev , said the diversity of voices at this year’s festival was particularly exciting, with Nigerian artists joining performers from Kenya, Canada and Brazil to create opportunities for audiences to experience different cultures and perspectives. entertainment.title: Uwaezu Kanu: Why Motherhood Feels Different for Women in Their 40s Today
entertainment.description: “Oh my God, Uwaezu! You need to hear the latest gist!” My younger sister buzzed with excitement. Though we had been living in different countries for a couple of years, we still made time to talk every single week. Unfortunately, when she called, I couldn’t talk on the phone as I had been ambushed by my kids, who were brandishing their homework and threatening to cry if I didn’t help them. As a mom herself, she immediately understood why I couldn’t continue with the conversation. I quickly made my excuses, and we laughed and hung up, promising to catch up at a more convenient time. However, that exchange got me thinking about how most millennial women have a radically different marriage and motherhood timeline from our mothers. You see, when my mother was in her early 40s, my siblings and I were in university, so she had a lot of free time during the week to spend relaxing, hanging out with her friends, and attending social events. Basically living her best life. I, on the other hand, at 40-plus, spend my days cooking pot after pot of hot meals that immediately get devoured by my ever-hungry kids, teaching my nursery school-aged kids how to count and spell, and trying but often failing to enforce a strict bedtime with yelling and threats. I constantly feel myself going underwater and have to fight for my life every single day. There are other ways motherhood has been such a hugely different experience for me than it was for my mother. Like many women of her generation, she got married right after secondary school as university education was not seen as vital. This meant that she was a teenage mother and so had more energy to spare on her kids. She also benefited from having a lot of support from domestic staff and relatives. I do not have any village supporting me with child-rearing. I have hired domestic staff in the past, but it was always one thing or another, and they ended up leaving me stranded. I also do not have youth on my side, and I have the back pain and other aches to prove it. But this experience is not unique to me. Statistics show that most women globally will have their first child at 30 or 31, and we are seeing a lot more women becoming first-time moms at 35 and above. sports.description: Alexander Zverev got off to a winning start in his ATP Finals campaign by beating Rafael Jodar in straight sets. Photo by Mathias Schulz/Newhouse Media/MB Media/Getty Images Jamie Murray reacts to Alexander Zverev beating Rafael Jodar It was a superb start for Zverev, but a tough day at the office for Jodar, who is coached by his father, Rafael Jodar Sr. Analysing the debutant’s performance on Sky Sports , former British player Jamie Murray said: “I think it was a tough match for him. “The fact that Zverev served as well as he did, he’s not giving him any chance to get into points and rally and build pressure that way. There’s always a lot of pressure on his own serve. It was a tough first out for him. I think he acquitted himself pretty well, really. I think he’s probably more excited about other matches that he’s got to come. “For me, it was just interesting to watch the dad. I sat a few seats down from him. Their relationship, how they go about things on the court, is very unique. I’m watching, and he’s looking for the dad a lot after a lot of points, especially ones that he loses. sports.description: The winning captains: Australia's Isabelle Kelly, her men's counterpart Isaah Yeo and England wheelchair skipper Lewis King [Getty Images] Has the 2026 Rugby League World Cup been a success or not? It depends on who you listen to - and perhaps where in the world you are. The men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments provided plenty of stories - from Kalyn Ponga's return from a broken arm in 23 days, to Jodie Cunningham's mangled ear, to the England wheelchair team's golden ladder, to the men's group format that caused widespread bafflement. But was the World Cup a triumph? The northern and southern hemisphere perspectives provide contrasting answers. For the fourth tournament running, Australia won the men's and women's titles, with New Zealand unable to deliver a twist in either final. Tonga and Samoa brought vibrancy and passion - performing to a level that underlined why they are being elevated to Tier One status. The large Polynesian population in the USA - which will co-host the 2030 men's and women's World Cups - is likely to be key in spreading the rugby league word further around the world. England's Wheelchair World Cup win, in a thunderous final against their old foes France, offset some of the disappointment felt when Brian McDermott's men and Stuart Barrow's women went home early. And unlike when the game was emerging from post-pandemic constraints in 2022, the tournament has also worked financially by posting a profit. "This whole tournament's been incredible," said Australia men's captain Isaah Yeo. "Not just the fans here for New Zealand and Australia, but just everyone. I thought it was all outstanding. "I think it's to date the most competitive and the best World Cup there's been. I think that's only going to continue to grow." That sentiment has been endorsed repeatedly by Australian television broadcaster Channel Seven, which paid a reported A$12m (£6.1m) for exclusive domestic free-to-air coverage of the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments. Not everyone has been able to feel that positivity, though. The decision to cut the men's tournament from 16 teams to 10 reduced the overall number of matches - and deprived teams such as Jamaica and Greece of a chance to build on the feelgood factor they provided as debutants in 2022. That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons. The only time Zverev looked troubled was when he went two break points down as he served for the opening set - before saving them with back-to-back aces. "I still think I have a lot of things to improve. It was not a perfect match but to start the tournament, I am very happy," the 29-year-old said. "Winning always helps, but it's been a good match." Zverev lost his first match as world number one at the Paris Masters in November and said afterwards he was "annoyed" at the reaction to his rise to the top of the rankings. Zverev underlined his status as the world's best player by walking out on court in Turin in a custom black leather jacket with a number one printed on the back. His performance was just as befitting of his position as he put constant pressure on the Jodar serve and dominated with his own first strike. The 20-year-old Jodar is one of the brightest talents in the men's game, having started the year outside the world's top 150. Now ranked 11th, he fought hard to stay in touch with Zverev, but could find no way through his serve. sports.title: When Michael Jordan’s agent revealed Nike’s $3 million fail-safe if Bulls legend flopped
sports.description: Photo by Bongarts/Getty Images Nike took all measures in Michael Jordan failed to become a global basketball superstar. When the Chicago Bulls selected Michael Jordan using the third overall pick in the 1984 NBA Draft, no one knew he would become a global sensation. Evidently, when Jordan signed a groundbreaking deal with Nike that included a signature shoe and royalties, it shocked the NBA community to its core. At the time, Nike wasn’t a gigantic corporation, and if trusting MJ had failed, it could have spelt trouble for the company. As a result, Nike tried to play it safe, as revealed by MJ’s agent, David Falk. David Falk once revealed Nike’s escape clause for Michael Jordan During a 2023 appearance on ‘The 20 & 20 Podcast,’ Falk revealed details about his conversation with Nike’s then-marketing head, Rob Strasser. Falk revealed how Nike wanted to insert stat-based clauses in Jordan’s contract with the sneaker company. “That makes no sense. You’re not an NBA team; what do you care what his statistics are? All you should care about is how many shoes he’s selling. “He said, ‘I’ll give you a number. If in the end of the third year, as we head into the fourth year, if we haven’t sold $3 million worth of shoes, we want to be able to stop making the shoe.’ I said no problem,” Falk recalled. He added, “We’ll honor the contract for the full five years, we’ll pay him every dollar he’s owed, but if he doesn’t make Rookie of the Year in his rookie year, or in the first three years, he doesn’t average 20 points a game ever, doesn’t ever make the All-Star team, we want to be able to stop making the shoe.” That $3 million target was Nike’s fail-safe in case Jordan never became a superstar. However, Falk then revealed how the Chicago Bulls guard smashed Nike’s expectations. “They thought selling 3 million will be like hitting a grand slam home run, and Michael sold 126 million in the first year. He sold roughly 40 percent probably of all Nike shoes,” Falk stated. Today, the Jordan Brand is a massive money-making machine for Nike and reportedly generates over $7 billion in annual revenue. sports.title: San Antonio is most popular location for an NFL team expansion, survey finds

Whitaker/San Antonio Express-News) San Antonio is the city NFL fans most want to see get a team, a new survey found. Nineteen percent of the 1,000 NFL fans surveyed by Betway Insider said they would like to see a franchise in the Alamo City, making it the most popular choice for an expansion team. San Antonio edged out Oklahoma City by just seven votes, despite both cities receiving 19% of the vote. The Lone Star state already has two NFL teams, the Dallas Cowboys and Houston Texans, but that didn't stop fans from calling for more. Austin took fifth place in the survey, with 14% of respondents saying they'd like to see a team there. READ MORE : 5 final thoughts from Cowboys-49ers: Can Dallas earn respect with upset of San Francisco? There have been periodic discussions among National Football League executives about expanding the league, but no new team has joined since 2002, when the Houston Texans were established. Thirteen percent of respondents said they don't think expansion is currently necessary. International expansion was the least popular among respondents. Just 9% of voters said London, which has hosted more NFL games than any other international city, should have its own team. Dublin and Munich received 4% and 2% of the vote, respectively. But even if the NFL were to expand, San Antonio faces several hurdles. The Alamodome lacks revenue-generating amenities like luxury suites and club seating, meaning San Antonio would likely need a new stadium to accommodate an NFL team. technology.title: LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in
technology.description: Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all. The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children. The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories." Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids. Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it. LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013 . It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge . The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011 . The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory. The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948 . EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I . ®

science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
science.description: null On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) Why it mattered When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later. "In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus." The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO. The Green Bank Telescope collapse left a mass of twisted debris behind. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions. "One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

science.title: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
science.description: null For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle. Why is it so challenging to predict T. CrB's nova flare? "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued. Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth. An animation of T. CrB brightening. (Image credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab) "The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold." Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event. science.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
science.description: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year. On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit) , 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life. On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event. By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August. Telling the tale of a dirty snowball Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space. Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten. "We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement . science.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
science.description: null Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off. Long-distance view of Ship's historic landing on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved. Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." The F light 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX. And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. Elon Musk has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average. Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites . And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring one million spacecraft , if all goes to plan. For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in low Earth orbit (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment. And that gets us back to the "work left to do" discussion, for SpaceX has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight with either Super Heavy or Ship. science.title: 'Alien: Fireteam Elite 2' is a good old-fashioned bug hunt, ironically plagued by bugs
science.description: The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games , and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel. At Summer Game Fest 2026 , we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong? Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years. Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2 's pure survival horror to look forward to. Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason. Another glorious day in the Corps (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat. This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. Fireteam Elite 2 is smart enough to sidestep fake tension and just hit the ground running. (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) All the design changes and upgrades reinforce the intent to make the ultimate Aliens action game. Classes have more defined roles and access to better, more destructive sci-fi weapons, and the upgrade to four-player fireteams is welcome when aliens and hostile synths won't stop pouring in. Tired of replaying campaign missions on higher difficulties and with modifiers? Prepare for the worst in this shooter's version of the classic horde mode. At its best, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 understands why James Cameron's masterpiece still holds up. During the biggest Xenomorph onslaughts — when the bullets are flying and acid is spraying — the game's shortcomings and jankier elements fade away. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
science.description: null On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier. The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old. The Apollo 12 astronauts on NASA's second crewed moon landing mission. They are (left to right) are Charles Conrad Jr., Richard F. Gordon Jr., and Alan L. Bean. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions. To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible. The Apollo 12 astronauts visited NASA's Surveyor 3 lander and took samples of it back to Earth. (Image credit: NASA) The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13. The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program. science.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video)
science.description: null SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse. "That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast today, his voice thick with emotion. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Space.com) The Ship catch occurred today at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time), roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off. Many SpaceX employees went outside to watch the vehicle, known as Ship 42, descend through the clouds toward its Starbase launch tower, which the company calls "Mechazilla." And they got quite a show: Ship 42 nestled gently into Mechazilla's waiting arms, while "Baby Come Back" played over SpaceX's landing webcast. "This is so incredible to see," SpaceX's Jessie Anderson said during the livestream. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes." Why was this such a big deal? SpaceX had already caught Super Heavy — on three previous Starship test flights, in fact. But it had never tried before with Ship. The upper stage is a tougher target, for it flies higher, farther and faster than the booster. Indeed, on Flight 15, Ship 42 came all the way back down from orbit. Ship 42 comes in for its landing on Nov. 14, 2026. science.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
science.description: null Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. How to measure distances in the night sky using your outstretched hand. (Image credit: Created in Canva Pro) Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA . Interested in seeing and capturing the planets for yourself? Then be sure to read our guide on everything you need to observe and photograph the planets of the solar system, along with our picks of the top telescopes , cameras and lenses for exploring the night sky in 2026. New Scientist covered things like the opening of Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. science.description: null STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO). SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The company called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear. A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy , which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The company previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights. SpaceX's Starship megarocket launches on its 15th test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Future/Josh Dinner, Space.com) Ship goes to orbit Ship's Raptors continued to fire following stage separation, completing their first burn just after eight minutes into flight. "We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during today's Flight 15 launch webcast. "That’s a really great moment."
